newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rain delays barley harvest in northeast France.
newsitem.headline: Rain delays barley harvest in northeast France.

text.p: Rain has delayed the start of the winter barley harvest in the Champagne-Ardennes region in northeastern France, cereals officials there said on Wednesday.
The harvest was due to have started on July 1 but wet weather for the past two weeks has pushed the potential date back to at least the weekend, government crop analysts said.
Now farmers are being warned not to start reaping the grain too suddenly as soon as the weather breaks, since below-average temperatures have left some plants below full maturity.
"The risk is that farmers will panic about the weather and start harvesting even when grain is not fully ripe," an official based in Chalons-sur-Marne, the region's cereals capital, said.

Farmers traditionally harvest sooner rather than later to avoid weather problems or unwanted germination in the fields, while cooperatives discourage deliveries of soggy or unripe grain, especially of malting barley.

On the other hand, leaving the harvest too late could encourage crop disease in such damp conditions, analysts said. Rainfall in the last growing stage has raised increasing concern over the quality of what is still certain to be a big crop.
Any chemicals put into the soil now would be too late.
"What we need is a week of good weather. If it continues wet like this for a few weeks there will be more and more quality worries," a local government crop official said.
Latest yield estimates are for around 7.1 tonnes per hectare for six-row winter barley and 6.8 tonnes for two-row winter barley, about unchanged from last year's good crop.
Latest area estimates for each type of grain are around 73,400 hectares for winter six-row barley, compared with 64,000 last year, and 36,600 hectares for two-row (against 34,500).
Yields for spring barley, harvested several weeks later, are pegged around 6.4 tonnes this year, down from 6.79 last year. About 104,000 hectares has been sown, up from 95,000 in 1996.
Crop analysts said some sodden barley plants were lying flat in the fields but this was not yet a serious problem.
Average regional yield forecasts for soft wheat were 8.1 tonnes per hectare, slightly down from 8.2 tonnes last year.
Analysts now think 427,000 hectares of winter and spring wheat was planted this year, down from 436,000 estimated by national cereals office ONIC last month but up from 413,500 last year.
The soft wheat harvest starts around late July.
